content: Cutis marmorata is a condition observed in newborns when they are exposed to cold environmental temperatures. It manifests as a transient, lacy, reticulated pattern of red and/or blue discoloration on the skin, covering most of the body. This vascular pattern is a heightened physiological vasomotor response, which typically diminishes as the child grows older. However, in some cases, it may still be noticeable in older children. Persistent and pronounced cutis marmorata is associated with certain genetic and systemic conditions, including Menkes disease, familial dysautonomia, Cornelia de Lange syndrome, trisomy 13, and trisomy 18. A related condition, cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita, presents with similar clinical features but is more severe. In this condition, the vascular lesions are more pronounced, may follow a segmental distribution, and are persistent. Additionally, it may be accompanied by complications such as dermal tissue loss, epidermal atrophy, and ulceration.
